The real lesson?

A move against the trend doesn't always mean the trend is reversing.

Sometimes, it simply shows that the opposing side hasn't gained enough strength.

Follow Candlesticks Decoded by @MotilalOswalLtd for more insights that help you decode the markets.

Here's the key difference between the two patterns:

Upside Tasuki Gap → Buyers may still have control.

Downside Tasuki Gap → Sellers may still have control.

In both cases, the third candle moves against the existing trend.

But the gap remains unfilled.

That's what makes these patterns interesting.

The third candle shows buyers attempting to push the price higher.

But they cannot completely close the gap created by the downward move.

This suggests that buying pressure may not be strong enough to reverse the trend.

The downtrend could continue.

📉 Downside Tasuki Gap

Now, reverse the situation.

This pattern appears during a downtrend.

A bearish candle establishes the downward move.

Another bearish candle opens below the previous candle, creating a gap.

A bullish candle follows, but fails to completely fill that gap.

Here's what that tells us. 👇

That third candle is where the story changes.

After two bullish candles, sellers enter and push the price lower.

But they cannot completely close the gap created by the previous move.

This suggests that selling pressure may not be strong enough to reverse the trend.

The uptrend could continue.

📈 Upside Tasuki Gap

This pattern appears during an uptrend.

It forms in 3 steps:

A bullish candle establishes the upward move.

Another bullish candle opens above the previous candle, creating a gap.

A bearish candle follows, but fails to completely fill that gap.

The interesting part? 👇

First, understand the gap.

When a stock is moving up, a gap up means its price opens significantly above the previous candle's range.

When it's moving down, a gap down means it opens significantly below the previous candle's range.

These gaps can reflect a strong shift in buying or selling pressure.

What if a candle moving against the trend is actually a sign that the trend could continue?

That's the interesting idea behind two candlestick patterns: the Upside Tasuki Gap and the Downside Tasuki Gap.

So when you see an index weight change, don’t look only at the stock price.

Ask:

Did the company’s market value change?
Did its free float change?
Or did the index methodology trigger a rebalance?

Sometimes, the answer is sitting in the ownership structure.

The key takeaway:

Index weights are not determined only by share prices.

They can also reflect changes in:

Company size
Publicly available shares
Liquidity

And the index provider’s methodology.

That’s why index construction is more dynamic than it may look.

And this matters to index funds.

If the index changes the stock’s weight, funds tracking that index generally need to adjust their holdings to continue tracking it.

So a change in ownership structure can eventually become a change in index exposure.

Here’s a simple example.

A company has:
₹1,000 crore market value

80% free float

Free-float market cap = ₹800 crore.

Now imagine the free-float factor falls to 60%.

With the same market value:

Free-float market cap = ₹600 crore.

The company has not become smaller.

But its investable portion has changed.

Corporate actions can also change the calculation.

For example:
• Mergers
• Acquisitions
• Share sales
• New share issuance
• Changes in strategic holdings

Index providers monitor such changes and apply their methodology.

So index weights are not necessarily permanent.

There’s another major event:

New shares can be issued.

But the impact depends on who receives them.

If new shares are issued to investors who qualify as public shareholders, free float may increase.

If they go to strategic or controlling holders, the free-float impact can be different.

The opposite can happen too.

Suppose a large shareholder increases its holding.

Shares that were previously available to the public may no longer count as free float under the methodology.

Free float can fall.

And the stock’s index weight may fall with it.

So what can actually change free float?

One common reason:

Promoters or large shareholders sell shares to the public.

More shares become available in the market.

Free float rises.

The company can therefore represent a larger portion of an index, depending on the index rules.

Remember the basic idea:

Free float = the portion of a company’s shares considered available to public investors under the index methodology.

So when that portion changes, the company’s free-float market capitalisation can change too.

And that can affect its index weight.

A company can stay the same.

Its share price can stay unchanged.

Yet its weight in an index can still change.

Why?

Because the number of shares available to the public can change.

That is where free float comes in. 🧵

𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗼𝗿 𝗩𝗶𝘇𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵, the Ahmedabad based CCTV and video surveillance company listed on NSE SME, has completed its preferential allotment. 13,63,600 equity shares were issued at ₹876 each, bringing in around ₹119.45 crore from 22 non-promoter investors.

Ashish Kacholia is the largest allottee in the round. He picked up 2,28,300 shares, which works out to almost exactly ₹20 crore, or about one-sixth of the entire issue. Post allotment, that translates to roughly 1.9% of the company.

A few things stood out to me while going through the list.

First, the quality of the allottee book. Alongside Kacholia, the round includes Motilal Oswal Financial Services (around ₹17.5 crore), LC Pharos Multi Strategy Fund (around ₹12.5 crore), Alchemy Long Term Ventures Fund and Capri Global Ventures (around ₹10 crore each), and Equirus IFSC Trust. It is not common to see this many institutional names in an SME preferential issue.

Second, the pricing history. Prizor came to market in July 2024 at ₹87. Warrants were issued in late 2025 at ₹291. This round is priced at ₹876. Investors have been willing to pay a meaningfully higher price at every stage, and the latest entry is roughly 10x the IPO price.

Third, the scale of the raise relative to the company's history. The IPO raised around ₹25 crore. This one round is close to five times that.

𝗣𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲
• The board had approved up to 15,13,600 shares for 24 investors in August. Two proposed allottees did not subscribe, so the final raise came in about ₹13 crore below the approved size.
• Once the outstanding warrants convert, promoter holding moves from around 67.9% to around 62%. Control is not in question, but the dilution is meaningful.

𝗠𝘆 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
Backing of this kind lends credibility to a small company, but it does not substitute for execution. At ₹876, a lot of optimism is already reflected in the price. From here, the story depends on how efficiently Prizor deploys this capital and whether revenue and margins scale accordingly. The next few quarterly results will tell us a lot.

Foreign investors may move billions out of India, but they're no longer the only force driving its stock market.

The rise of domestic investors has changed the equation, making India's markets less reliant on foreign money alone.

What's changed is the balance.

India's growing domestic investor base has created another major source of equity-market demand.

That means foreign outflows no longer tell the entire story of where the market might head next.

So, does foreign money still matter?

Absolutely.

Foreign investors bring capital, liquidity and global participation. 

Their buying and selling can influence market direction, valuations and sentiment.

India hasn't stopped needing foreign capital.

But don't mistake this for complete protection.

Domestic investors cannot prevent every correction. 

If selling intensifies or economic conditions weaken, Indian markets can still fall sharply.

Their presence can provide support, not a guarantee.

There's another important difference.

Foreign investors can shift money between countries based on global interest rates, currency movements and international risks.

Domestic investors, meanwhile, are investing in a market backed by India's own savings and growing participation.

This changes how the market responds to foreign selling.

When foreign investors sell, domestic institutions can use incoming funds to buy shares, helping cushion the impact.

The selling doesn't disappear, but its effect can be offset.

And SIPs have played a major role in this shift.

Every month, investors automatically channel money into mutual funds through Systematic Investment Plans.

Even when markets get volatile, these regular investments can keep domestic money flowing into equities.

But who exactly are these domestic investors?

Think of millions of Indians investing through mutual funds, SIPs and direct stock purchases.

Individually, their contributions may seem small. 

Together, they can move billions.

The answer lies closer to home.

While foreign investors were pulling money out, Indian investors were putting money in. 

Domestic money helped absorb the selling pressure and support the market.

Foreign investors poured $63.5 billion into Indian equities over 9 years, then pulled out nearly $63.6 billion in just 2. 

Yet India's stock market didn't collapse.

The Major Culprit Right Now?
"Brent Crude"!

Brent crude is around $113 a barrel today & we all know that we imports nearly 90% of its oil. At these levels the obvious happens : import bill rises, the rupee comes under pressure, and company costs go up.
India brings in roughly 4.9 million barrels a day. A $10 rise that stays can add about $18 billion to the annual import bill. More dollars go out & a weaker rupee makes the next barrel costlier.

On 22 October, when Brent crossed $112, Nifty fell 0.54% and Sensex dropped 0.62%. Oil was not the only reason, but it added to the selling.
Higher diesel and petrol raise costs across transport, raw materials and manufacturing. Companies with stronger pricing power and reasonable valuations are better placed. Expensive mid and small caps with thin margins could face a double hit from lower earnings and falling valuations. Logistics, auto parts, building materials and a lot of mid and small manufacturers fall in the group that absorbs more of the cost. Revenues can still grow while margins get squeezed.

Yes Upstream oil & gas producers gain from higher prices, but they are a small part of the index and of most portfolios. The net effect for the broader market stays negative when oil stays high.
The market is already cutting stock prices before the weaker margins even show up in quarterly results. That is why the reaction looks broader than just the obvious oil-sensitive names.
If Brent stays above $110 for weeks, the chance of earnings downgrades in H2 FY27 rises and foreign flows stay cautious. A move back towards $100 would ease some of the pressure on earnings expectations and market sentiment. A few days of expensive oil is manageable,but several months is a totally different story !
